title: Chapter 9 — Charadriiformes
description: A highly diverse order of shorebirds, gulls, terns, and auks united by a shared ancestry despite very different appearances and lifestyles. With over 350 species it is one of the largest bird orders. Most are associated with coastal and aquatic habitats and many make extraordinary migrations. Gulls and terns are among the most familiar seabirds of northern Europe, while the waders (sandpipers, plovers, snipe) are the defining birds of estuaries and mudflats.

children.name: Anous
children.description: Noddies — dark-plumaged tropical terns with distinctive pale or white caps, breeding on tropical islands across all three major oceans. Unlike most terns, noddies do not plunge-dive but snatch prey from the surface, and they often rest on the sea rather than staying constantly airborne.

children.name: Anous albivitta
children.description: The grey noddy or grey ternlet (Anous albivitta) is a seabird belonging to the family Laridae..

children.name: Anous ceruleus
children.description: The blue noddy or hinaokū or manuohina (Anous ceruleus) is a seabird in the family Laridae..

children.name: Anous minutus
children.description: The black noddy (Anous minutus), also known as white-capped noddy, is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Anous stolidus
children.description: The brown noddy, common noddy or noddy tern (Anous stolidus) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Anous tenuirostris
children.description: The lesser noddy (Anous tenuirostris), also known as the sooty noddy, is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Chlidonias
children.description: Marsh terns — dark-bodied freshwater terns that pick insects and small prey from the surface of marshes rather than plunge-diving.

children.name: Chlidonias niger
children.description: The black tern is a small tern generally found in or near inland water that breeds in Europe, Western Asia and North America. In winter the birds migrate to coastal areas of Africa and South America.

children.name: Chlidonias hybrida
children.description: The whiskered tern (Chlidonias hybrida) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Chlidonias leucopterus
children.description: The white-winged tern or white-winged black tern is a species of tern in the family Laridae. It is a small species generally found in or near bodies of fresh water across much of the world, including Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia. The genus name is from Ancient Greek khelidonios, "swallow-like", from khelidon, "swallow".

children.name: Chroicocephalus
children.description: Hooded and black-headed gulls — smaller than Larus, characterised in summer by dark hoods that range from black to chocolate brown. The black-headed gull (skrattmås) is the most numerous gull in Stockholm and across Sweden's inland waters: its breeding colonies produce a cacophony of laughing calls that give it its Swedish name ('skratt' = laugh). Despite the name, the summer hood is actually dark chocolate brown, not black. Black-headed gulls are inland birds as much as coastal ones, following ploughs, roosting on city parks, and commuting between feeding areas and inland reservoirs in spectacular evening flights.

children.name: Chroicocephalus hartlaubii
children.description: Hartlaub's gull (Chroicocephalus hartlaubii) is a small gull in the genus Chroicocephalus..

children.name: Chroicocephalus minutus
children.description: The world's smallest gull at just 28 cm. Black underwing and black hood in summer. Breeds in Scandinavian and Baltic marshes. Occurs regularly on passage along Swedish coasts. Has a delicate, tern-like flight, dipping to the surface to pick off insects.

children.name: Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae
children.description: The silver gull (Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae) is a gull in Oceania.

children.name: Chroicocephalus ridibundus
children.description: The black-headed gull is a small gull that breeds in much of the Palearctic in Europe and Asia, and also locally in smaller numbers in coastal eastern Canada. Most of the population is migratory and winters further south, but many also remain in the milder areas of northwestern Europe. It was formerly sometimes cited as "common black-headed gull" to distinguish it from "great black-headed gull".

children.name: Chroicocephalus saundersi
children.description: Saunders's gull (Saundersilarus saundersi) or Chinese black-headed gull, is a species of gull in the family Laridae..

children.name: Chroicocephalus serranus
children.description: The Andean gull (Chroicocephalus serranus) is a species in subfamily Larinae of the family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers.

children.name: Creagrus
children.description: Creagrus - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Creagrus furcatus
children.description: The swallow-tailed gull (Creagrus furcatus) is an equatorial seabird in the gull family, Laridae..

children.name: Feducciavis
children.description: Feducciavis - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Gaviota
children.description: Gaviota - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Gaviota niobrara
children.description: Gaviota niobrara is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Miocene..

children.name: Gelochelidon
children.description: Gull-billed terns — stout, short-billed terns that hawk insects and small vertebrates over land as well as water.

children.name: Gelochelidon macrotarsa
children.description: The Australian tern or Australian gull-billed tern (Gelochelidon macrotarsa) is a tern in the family Laridae, native to Australia..

children.name: Gygis
children.description: White terns — ethereally beautiful, entirely snow-white tropical seabirds that famously lay their single egg on a bare branch with no nest. The large blue eye and translucent wings give them an otherworldly appearance.

children.name: Gygis alba
children.description: The Atlantic white tern (Gygis alba), also known as the common white tern, is a small seabird found in the Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Hydrocoloeus
children.description: Hydrocoloeus - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Hydrocoloeus minutus
children.description: The little gull (Hydrocoloeus minutus) is a species of gull belonging to the family Laridae which is mainly found in the Palearctic with some small colonies in North America..

children.name: Hydroprogne
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Caspian tern, the largest tern in the world.

children.name: Hydroprogne caspia
children.description: The Caspian tern is the world's largest species of tern, with a subcosmopolitan but scattered distribution. Despite its extensive range, it is monotypic of its genus, and has no accepted subspecies. The genus name is from Ancient Greek hudro-, "water-", and Latin progne, "swallow".

children.name: Ichthyaetus
children.description: Large dark-hooded gulls of southern Eurasia and Africa, several with striking black or grey hoods in breeding plumage.

children.name: Ichthyaetus hemprichii
children.description: The sooty gull (Ichthyaetus hemprichii) is a species of gull in the family Laridae, also known as the Aden gull or Hemprich's gull.

children.name: Ichthyaetus melanocephalus
children.description: The Mediterranean gull (Ichthyaetus melanocephalus) is a small gull.

children.name: Ichthyaetus relictus
children.description: The relict gull or Central Asian gull (Ichthyaetus relictus) is a medium-sized gull.

children.name: Larosterna
children.description: A monotypic genus containing only the Inca tern, one of the most striking and unusual seabirds in the world, unique to the cold Humboldt Current system of the South American Pacific coast.

children.name: Larosterna inca
children.description: The Inca tern (Larosterna inca) is a near-threatened species of tern in the subfamily Sterninae of the family Laridae (the gulls, terns, and skimmers).

children.name: Larus
children.description: Large gulls — the dominant seabirds of northern European coastlines and the most familiar waterbirds in Swedish cities. Gulls are supremely opportunistic generalists: they eat fish, invertebrates, carrion, garbage, and other birds' eggs and chicks with equal facility. Their intelligence is remarkable — herring gulls have been documented dropping shellfish onto hard surfaces to break them open, and individuals can recognise specific human faces. Stockholm's rocky archipelago supports large colonies of herring gulls and lesser black-backed gulls, whose calls are the ambient soundtrack of the Swedish coast. 'Gull identification' has become one of birding's most obsessive niches, with hybrids, unusual ages, and rare visitors drawing dedicated specialists.

children.name: Larus argentatus
children.description: The European herring gull or simply herring gull is a large gull, up to 66 cm (26 in) long. It breeds throughout the northern and western coasts of Europe. Some European herring gulls, especially those resident in colder areas, migrate farther south in winter, but many are permanent residents, such as in Ireland, Britain, Iceland, or on the North Sea shores.

children.name: Larus armenicus
children.description: The Armenian gull (Larus armenicus) is a large gull found in the Caucasus and the Middle East.

children.name: Larus barabensis
children.description: The lesser black-backed gull (Larus fuscus) is a large gull that breeds on the Atlantic and Arctic coasts of Europe.

children.name: Larus belcheri
children.description: Belcher's gull, also known as the band-tailed gull, is a bird in the family Laridae found along the Pacific coast of South America. It formerly included the very similar Olrog's gull as a subspecies, but that bird occurs on the Atlantic coast of South America and is now accepted as a separate species Larus atlanticus. Belcher's gull is a medium-sized gull with a blackish mantle, white head and underparts, a black band on the otherwise white tail, and a yellow bill with a red and black tip.

children.name: Larus bulleri
children.description: The black-billed gull (Chroicocephalus bulleri), also called Buller's gull or tarāpuka (Māori), is a Near Threatened species of gull in the family Laridae..

children.name: Larus cachinnans
children.description: The Caspian gull is a large gull and a member of the herring and lesser black-backed gull complex. The scientific name is from Latin. Larus appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird, and cachinnans means 'laughing', from cachinnare 'to laugh'.

children.name: Larus californicus
children.description: The California gull (Larus californicus) is a medium-sized gull, smaller on average than the herring gull, but larger on average than the ring-billed gull (though it may overlap in size with both).

children.name: Larus canus
children.description: The common gull is a gull that breeds in cool temperate regions of the Palearctic from Iceland and Scotland east to Kamchatka in the Russian Far East. Most common gulls migrate further south in winter, reaching the Mediterranean Sea, the southern Caspian Sea, and the seas around China and Japan; northwest European populations are at least partly resident. The closely related short-billed gull was formerly often included in this species, which was then sometimes known collectively as "mew gull".

children.name: Larus dominicanus
children.description: The kelp gull (Larus dominicanus), also known as the Dominican gull, is a gull that breeds on coasts and islands through much of the Southern Hemisphere.

children.name: Larus elmorei
children.description: Larus elmorei is an extinct species of gull that lived during the mid-Pliocene..

children.name: Larus fuscus
children.description: The lesser black-backed gull is a large gull that breeds on the Atlantic and Arctic coasts of Europe. It is migratory, wintering from the British Isles south to West Africa. However, it has increased dramatically in North America, especially along the east coast.

children.name: Larus glaucoides
children.description: The Iceland gull (Larus glaucoides) is a medium-sized gull that breeds in the Arctic regions of Canada and Greenland, but not in Iceland (as its name suggests), where it is only seen during winter.

children.name: Larus hyperboreus
children.description: The glaucous gull is a large gull, the second-largest gull in the world. The genus name is from Latin larus, which appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird. The specific name hyperboreus is Latin for "northern" from the Ancient Greek Huperboreoi people from the far north "Glaucous" is from Latin glaucus and denotes the grey colour of the gull.

children.name: Larus lacus
children.description: Larus lacus is an extinct species of gull that lived in North America during the Late Pliocene..

children.name: Larus marinus
children.description: The great black-backed gull (Larus marinus) is the largest member of the gull and tern family Laridae.

children.name: Larus michahellis
children.description: The yellow-legged gull or western yellow-legged gull is a large gull found in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, which has only recently achieved wide recognition as a distinct species. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of either the Caspian gull L. cachinnans, or more broadly as a subspecies of the herring gull L.

children.name: Larus naumanni
children.description: A large, pale-mantled gull of Mongolian and Chinese plateau lakes, closely allied to the yellow-legged gull complex. Breeds on high-altitude inland lakes across Mongolia and adjacent China, and winters along the coasts of eastern China and Korea. Only recently widely accepted as a full species separate from the Caspian gull, following genetic analysis.

children.name: Larus occidentalis
children.description: The western gull (Larus occidentalis) is a large white-headed gull that lives on the west coast of North America and the Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Larus oregonus
children.description: Larus oregonus is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Late Pleistocene..

children.name: Larus pacificus
children.description: The Pacific gull (Larus pacificus) is a gull, native to the coasts of Australia.

children.name: Larus perpetuus
children.description: Larus perpetuus is an extinct species of gull that lived in North America during the Pliocene..

children.name: Larus robustus
children.description: Larus robustus is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Late Pleistocene..

children.name: Larus utunui
children.description: The Huahine gull (Chroicocephalus utunui), also known as the Society Islands gull, is an extinct bird, a species of gull of which subfossil bones were found at the Fa'ahia archeological site on Huahine, in the Society Islands of French Polynesia..

children.name: Larus vegae
children.description: The Vega gull, East Siberian gull, or East Siberian herring gull (Larus vegae) is a large gull of the herring gull/lesser black-backed gull complex which breeds in Northeast Asia.

children.name: Leucophaeus
children.description: American hooded gulls including the abundant laughing gull and the desert-nesting grey gull.

children.name: Leucophaeus atricilla
children.description: The laughing gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) is a medium-sized gull of North and South America.

children.name: Leucophaeus modestus
children.description: The grey gull, also known as garuma gull (Leucophaeus modestus), is a medium-sized gull native to South America.

children.name: Leucophaeus fuliginosus
children.description: The lava gull (Leucophaeus fuliginosus), also known as the dusky gull, and is the rarest gull in the world.

children.name: Leucophaeus scoresbii
children.description: The dolphin gull (Leucophaeus scoresbii), sometimes erroneously called the red-billed gull (a somewhat similar but unrelated species from New Zealand), is a gull native to southern Chile and Argentina, and the Falkland Islands.

children.name: Onychoprion
children.description: Tropical seabird terns with dark upperparts that spend years continuously at sea before returning to breed on remote islands.

children.name: Onychoprion fuscatus
children.description: The sooty tern (Onychoprion fuscatus) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Onychoprion aleuticus
children.description: The Aleutian tern is a migratory bird living in the subarctic region of the globe most of the year. It is frequently associated with the Arctic tern, which it closely resembles. While both species have a black cap, the Aleutian tern may be distinguished by its white forehead.

children.name: Onychoprion anaethetus
children.description: The bridled tern (Onychoprion anaethetus) is a seabird of the family Laridae.

children.name: Onychoprion lunatus
children.description: The spectacled tern (Onychoprion lunatus), also known as the grey-backed tern, is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Pagophila
children.description: A monotypic genus for the ivory gull, the only entirely white gull, tied to the high Arctic pack ice.

children.name: Pagophila eburnea
children.description: The ivory gull (Pagophila eburnea) is a small gull, the only species in the genus Pagophila.

children.name: Phaetusa
children.description: Phaetusa - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Phaetusa simplex
children.description: The large-billed tern (Phaetusa simplex) is a species of tern in the family Laridae..

children.name: Procelsterna
children.description: Blue noddies — tiny, pale terns of the tropical Pacific, the most delicate members of the Laridae, feeding on zooplankton and tiny fish by dipping to the sea surface.

children.name: Procelsterna cerulea
children.description: The blue noddy or hinaokū or manuohina (Anous ceruleus) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Procelsterna albivitta
children.description: thumb|250px|At rookery in northern New Zealand.

children.name: Pseudosterna
children.description: Pseudosterna - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rhodostethia
children.description: Rhodostethia - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rhodostethia rosea
children.description: Ross's gull (Rhodostethia rosea) is a small gull, the only species in its genus, although it has been suggested the genus should be merged with the closely related Hydrocoloeus, which otherwise only includes the little gull..

children.name: Rissa
children.description: Kittiwakes — small, gentle, truly pelagic gulls that nest on sheer sea cliffs and spend the rest of the year far out at sea.

children.name: Rissa estesi
children.description: Rissa estesi is an extinct species of bird in the genus Rissa that lived during the Piacenzian stage of the Neogene period..

children.name: Rissa tridactyla
children.description: The black-legged kittiwake is a seabird species in the gull family Laridae. This species was first described by Carl Linnaeus in his landmark 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae as Larus tridactylus. The English name is derived from its call, a shrill 'kittee-wa-aaake, kitte-wa-aaake'.

children.name: Rynchops
children.description: Skimmers — unique terns with a lower mandible longer than the upper, used to slice through the water surface in flight to snap up fish.

children.name: Rynchops albicollis
children.description: The Indian skimmer (Rynchops albicollis) or Indian scissors-bill, is one of the three species that belong to the skimmer genus Rynchops in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rynchops flavirostris
children.description: The African skimmer is a species of bird belonging to the skimmer genus Rynchops in the family Laridae. It is found along rivers, lakes and lagoons in Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Rynchops niger
children.description: The black skimmer (Rynchops niger) is a tern-like seabird, one of three similar bird species in the skimmer genus Rynchops in the gull family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna
children.description: Sea terns — elegant, sharply pointed seabirds built for plunge-diving into the sea for small fish. Terns are the migrants par excellence: the Arctic tern (silvertärna) makes the longest migration of any animal on Earth, breeding in the Arctic (including northern Sweden's coast) and wintering in the Antarctic, covering 70,000–90,000 km annually — it experiences more daylight than any other creature. Common terns (fisktärna) breed in noisy, fiercely defensive colonies on Swedish coastal rocks and lake islands. Terns dive at speed into the water to catch fish, folding their wings at the last moment. Their aggressive colony defence — dive-bombing and occasionally striking intruders — makes tern colonies an exciting experience for visiting naturalists.

children.name: Sterna aurantia
children.description: , Karnataka]] The river tern or Indian river tern (Sterna aurantia) is a tern in the family Laridae, the largest species currently included in the genus Sterna of typical terns.

children.name: Sterna dougallii
children.description: The roseate tern (Sterna dougallii) is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna hirundinacea
children.description: The South American tern (Sterna hirundinacea) is a species of tern found in coastal regions of southern South America, including the Falkland Islands, ranging north to Peru (Pacific coast) and Brazil (Atlantic coast)..

children.name: Sterna hirundo
children.description: The common tern is a seabird in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar distribution, its four subspecies breeding in temperate and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America. It is strongly migratory, wintering in coastal tropical and subtropical regions.

children.name: Sterna paradisaea
children.description: The Arctic tern is a tern in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar breeding distribution covering the Arctic and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. The species is strongly migratory, seeing two summers each year as it migrates along a convoluted route from its northern breeding grounds to the Antarctic coast for the southern summer and back again about six months later.

children.name: Sterna sandvicensis
children.description: The Sandwich tern (Thalasseus sandvicensis) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna trudeaui
children.description: The snowy-crowned tern (Sterna trudeaui), also known as Trudeau's tern, is a species of bird in subfamily Sterninae of the family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers..

children.name: Sterna virgata
children.description: The Kerguelen tern (Sterna virgata) is a tern of the Southern Hemisphere..

children.name: Sterna vittata
children.description: The Antarctic tern (Sterna vittata) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula
children.description: The smallest terns — fast-flying, yellow-billed species that hover and plunge into shallow water for tiny fish.

children.name: Sternula albifrons
children.description: The little tern (Sternula albifrons) is a seabird of the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula antillarum
children.description: The least tern (Sternula antillarum) is a species of tern that breeds in North America and locally in northern South America.

children.name: Sternula balaenarum
children.description: The Damara tern (Sternula balaenarum) is a species of small tern in the family Laridae which breeds in the southern summer in southern Africa and migrates to tropical African coasts to winter.

children.name: Sternula lorata
children.description: The Peruvian tern (Sternula lorata) is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula nereis
children.description: The fairy tern (Sternula nereis) is a small tern which is native to the southwestern Pacific.

children.name: Sternula sinensis
children.description: A critically endangered small tern breeding on a tiny number of sandy beaches in China, Taiwan, and the Philippines. The global population is estimated at just a few thousand birds and has been severely impacted by coastal development. Conservation efforts in Taiwan using artificial nesting platforms have produced encouraging results.

children.name: Thalasseus
children.description: Crested terns — large terns with shaggy black crests and slender bills, plunge-diving for fish in warm and temperate seas.

children.name: Thalasseus albididorsalis
children.description: The West African crested tern (Thalasseus albididorsalis) is a bird species in the family Laridae..

children.name: Thalasseus bengalensis
children.description: The lesser crested tern (Thalasseus bengalensis) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus bergii
children.description: The greater crested tern (Thalasseus bergii), also called crested tern, swift tern, or great crested tern, is a tern in the family Laridae that nests in dense colonies on coastlines and islands in the tropical and subtropical Old World.

children.name: Thalasseus bernsteini
children.description: The Chinese crested tern (Thalasseus bernsteini) is a tern in the family Laridae..

children.name: Thalasseus elegans
children.description: The elegant tern (Thalasseus elegans) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus maximus
children.description: The royal tern (Thalasseus maximus) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus sandvicensis
children.description: The Sandwich tern is a tern in the family Laridae. It is very closely related to the lesser crested tern, Chinese crested tern, Cabot's tern, and elegant tern and has been known to interbreed with both elegant and lesser crested terns. It breeds in the Palearctic from Europe to the Caspian Sea, and winters in the Mediterranean and on the coasts of Africa, India, and Sri Lanka.

children.name: Thalasseus zimmermanni
children.description: One of the world's rarest birds — fewer than 100 individuals are known to exist — breeding only on a handful of rocky islands off China and Taiwan. Distinguished from the greater crested tern by its yellow bill with a black tip and white-based black crest. Rediscovered breeding in 2000 after 63 years without confirmed records; listed as Critically Endangered.

children.name: Xema
children.description: A monotypic genus for Sabine's gull, a small, tern-like Arctic gull with a boldly patterned wing.

children.name: Numenius
children.description: Curlews — large, long-billed waders whose haunting, liquid calls are among the most evocative sounds in the natural world. The Eurasian curlew is one of Sweden's most recognisable waders, its long decurved bill perfectly adapted for probing into mud, peat, and grass root zones to extract earthworms, insects, and crustaceans. The bubbling song of the curlew, delivered in soaring display flight over boggy farmland and coastal meadows, is the defining sound of the Swedish countryside in spring — but it is a sound that is becoming scarcer as agricultural intensification and drainage destroy the wet grasslands the curlew requires for nesting.

children.name: Numenius arquata
children.description: The Eurasian curlew or common curlew is a very large wader in the family Scolopacidae. It is one of the most widespread of the curlews, breeding across temperate Europe and Asia. In Europe, this species is often referred to just as the "curlew", and in Scotland known as the "whaup" in Scots.

children.name: Numenius phaeopus
children.description: The Eurasian whimbrel, historically known as the white-rumped whimbrel in North America, is a wader in the large family Scolopacidae. It is one of the most widespread of the curlews, breeding across much of subarctic Palearctic region and Europe as far south as Scotland. This species and the Hudsonian whimbrel were split in 2019, although some taxonomic authorities still consider them to be conspecific.

children.name: Numenius hudsonicus
children.description: The Hudsonian whimbrel or Hudsonian curlew (Numenius hudsonicus) is a wader in the large family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Numenius minutus
children.description: The little curlew (Numenius minutus) is a wader in the large bird family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Numenius borealis
children.description: The Eskimo curlew (Numenius borealis), also known as northern curlew, is a species of curlew in the family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Limosa
children.description: Godwits — large waders with long, straight or slightly upturned bills, named from the Old English for 'good' and a word for their cry. Four species constitute this genus, and all are renowned for extraordinary long-distance migrations. The bar-tailed godwit holds the world record for non-stop bird flight, covering over 12,000 km from Alaska to New Zealand without landing. In breeding plumage godwits are strikingly coloured in rich chestnut and brick red; in winter they adopt plain grey-brown tones. Several species have experienced steep population declines due to loss of intertidal habitats at staging sites.

children.name: Limosa limosa
children.description: The black-tailed godwit is a large, long-legged, long-billed shorebird first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1758. It is a member of the godwit genus, Limosa. There are four subspecies, all with orange head, neck and chest in breeding plumage and dull grey-brown winter coloration, and distinctive black and white wingbar at all times.

children.name: Limosa lapponica
children.description: The bar-tailed godwit is a large and strongly migratory wader in the family Scolopacidae, which feeds on bristle-worms and shellfish on coastal mudflats and estuaries. It has distinctive red breeding plumage, long legs, and a long upturned bill. Bar-tailed godwits breed on Arctic coasts and tundra from Scandinavia to Alaska, and overwinter on coasts in temperate and tropical regions of Australia and New Zealand.

children.name: Limosa haemastica
children.description: The Hudsonian godwit (Limosa haemastica) is a large shorebird in the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae.

children.name: Limosa fedoa
children.description: The marbled godwit (Limosa fedoa) is a large migratory shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Gallinago
children.description: Snipe — cryptically streaked marsh birds whose remarkable aerial displays produce one of the most unusual sounds in the animal kingdom. The common snipe is a master of camouflage, its brown-and-buff streaked plumage rendering it almost invisible among sedge and rush as it stands motionless. When flushed it explodes from underfoot in a fast, erratic, zigzagging flight that historically made it the most challenging of all quarry species for hunters — giving rise to the word 'sniper'. In spring, male snipe perform 'drumming' or 'bleating' display dives over their territories: as the bird stoops at speed, the two outermost tail feathers spread and vibrate in the airstream to produce a distinctive pulsing sound audible for hundreds of metres.

children.name: Gallinago gallinago
children.description: The common snipe is a small, stocky wader native to the Old World, where it breeds in marshes, bogs, tundra and wet meadows. It is usually shy and well-camouflaged, foraging in soft mud mainly for insects and earthworms but also some plant material. During courtship, males perform a "winnowing" display; flying high in circles and then taking shallow dives to produce a "drumming" sound by vibrating the tail feathers.

children.name: Gallinago megala
children.description: Swinhoe's snipe, also known as forest snipe or Chinese snipe, is a medium-sized, long-billed, migratory wader.

children.name: Gallinago nigripennis
children.description: The African snipe (Gallinago nigripennis) also known as the Ethiopian snipe, is a small stocky wader.

children.name: Gallinago macrodactyla
children.description: The Madagascar snipe (Gallinago macrodactyla) is a small stocky wader.

children.name: Gallinago media
children.description: The great snipe is a small stocky wader in the genus Gallinago. This bird's breeding habitat is marshes and wet meadows with short vegetation in north-eastern Europe, including north-western Russia. Great snipes are migratory, wintering in Africa.

children.name: Gallinago undulata
children.description: The giant snipe (Gallinago undulata) is a stocky wader.

children.name: Gallinago stricklandii
children.description: The Fuegian snipe (Gallinago stricklandii) also known as the cordilleran snipe, is a small stocky wader.

children.name: Gallinago imperialis
children.description: | range_map = Gallinago imperialis map.svg.

children.name: Gallinago nemoricola
children.description: thumb|Wood Snipe, [[Thailand]] The wood snipe (Gallinago nemoricola) is a species of snipe which breeds in the Himalayas of northern India, Nepal, Bhutan and southern China.

children.name: Gallinago solitaria
children.description: The solitary snipe (Gallinago solitaria) is a small stocky wader.

children.name: Gallinago andina
children.description: The puna snipe (Gallinago andina) is a bird in tribe Scolopancinai and subfamily Scolopacinae of family Scolopacidae, the sandpipers and relatives.

children.name: Gallinago paraguaiae
children.description: The Pantanal snipe (Gallinago paraguaiae) is a bird in tribe Scolopancinai and subfamily Scolopacinae of family Scolopacidae, the sandpipers and relatives.

children.name: Gallinago nobilis
children.description: The noble snipe (Gallinago nobilis) is a small stocky wader.

children.name: Lymnocryptes
children.description: Jack snipe — a monotypic genus containing only the jack snipe, the smallest member of the Scolopacidae and one of the most secretive and camouflaged of all waders. Sometimes included within Gallinago, Lymnocryptes is treated as distinct based on its unique morphology, behaviour, and molecular data. The jack snipe has a distinctly different tail structure from Gallinago snipe, with a pointed central tail and different outer tail feather morphology. Its extreme reluctance to flush and habit of 'freezing' motionless in vegetation has made it one of the most challenging waders to study.

children.name: Lymnocryptes minima
children.description: The world's smallest snipe and one of its most cryptic birds, relying entirely on camouflage and freezing behaviour rather than flight for predator avoidance. Breeds in boggy subarctic forest from Scandinavia to Siberia; winters south to tropical Africa and South Asia. Males perform a remarkable ground display resembling the galloping of a horse — a repetitive four-beat sound produced mechanically — giving rise to one of its folk names 'horse snipe'. The bouncing feeding action caused by compressed body movements is highly distinctive.

children.name: Coenocorypha
children.description: New Zealand snipe — a genus of small, cryptic snipe endemic to the remote islands of New Zealand and its subantarctic territories. These birds evolved in isolation following colonisation of the southwestern Pacific by a Gallinago ancestor, diverging into several island-specific forms. Coenocorypha snipe are characterised by their extremely short wings and almost flightless habits on their predator-free island homes; several island populations were extirpated following the introduction of rats and other predators. The surviving species perform remarkable nocturnal aerial display flights, producing sounds with their outer tail feathers — a behaviour paralleling the 'drumming' of their Gallinago relatives.

children.name: Coenocorypha aucklandica
children.description: The Subantarctic snipe (Coenocorypha aucklandica), sometimes also Auckland snipe or New Zealand snipe, is a species of snipe endemic to New Zealand's subantarctic islands.

children.name: Coenocorypha huegeli
children.description: The Snares snipe (Coenocorypha huegeli), also known as the Snares Island snipe, or tutukiwi in Māori, is a species of bird in the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae.

children.name: Scolopax
children.description: Woodcocks — the most terrestrial of the sandpipers, inhabiting damp woodland and forest rather than open wetlands. The Eurasian woodcock is one of the most enigmatic birds in the temperate Holarctic: its cryptic dead-leaf plumage makes it essentially invisible on the forest floor, and it is almost exclusively nocturnal. The one exception is the spectacular 'roding' display flight performed by males at dusk and dawn throughout spring: the male follows a regular circuit over the woodland canopy, uttering a series of deep grunting 'orr-orr-orr' sounds alternating with a high squeaky 'twick'. Woodcocks have eyes positioned high on the sides of their head, giving 360-degree vision — a complete field of view without turning their head.

children.name: Scolopax rusticola
children.description: The Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola) is a medium-small wading bird found in temperate and subarctic Eurasia.

children.name: Scolopax saturata
children.description: The Javan woodcock (Scolopax saturata) is a small, long-billed bird in the family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Scolopax bukidnonensis
children.description: The Bukidnon woodcock (Scolopax bukidnonensis), or Philippine woodcock is a medium-sized wader.

children.name: Scolopax celebensis
children.description: The Sulawesi woodcock (Scolopax celebensis) also known as Celebes woodcock, is a medium-sized wader.

children.name: Scolopax rochussenii
children.description: The Moluccan woodcock (Scolopax rochussenii), also known as the Obi woodcock, is a lowland wader endemic to Indonesia.

children.name: Scolopax mira
children.description: The Amami woodcock (Scolopax mira) is a medium-sized wader.

children.name: Scolopax minor
children.description: The American woodcock (Scolopax minor), sometimes colloquially referred to as the timberdoodle, mudbat, becasse, bogsucker, brush snipe, night partridge, or Labrador twister is a small shorebird species found primarily in the eastern half of North America.

children.name: Scolopax javaensis
children.description: A poorly known woodcock endemic to the island of Java in Indonesia, inhabiting montane forest at elevations above 1,000 m in the volcanic highland interior. One of the least-studied of all woodcocks; very few confirmed observations exist and most of what is known about the species comes from specimens collected in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Like other island-endemic Scolopax woodcocks, it is classified as Vulnerable due to ongoing deforestation in its restricted range.

children.name: Scolopax scutulata
children.description: A large, dark woodcock of montane forest in the Greater Sundas and adjacent islands of Indonesia, closely related to the Eurasian woodcock but considerably larger and darker in plumage. Inhabits dense primary and secondary montane forest above 1,200 m in Sumatra, Borneo, and the Philippines. One of the more imposing woodcock species but poorly known due to its nocturnal habits and dense forest habitat; its roding display flights have rarely been described.

children.name: Tringa
children.description: Shanks, tattlers, and their allies — medium-sized, long-legged waders of wetland edges and mudflats that are among the most familiar waders in the Holarctic. The group contains some of the most abundant breeding waders in Scandinavia (redshank, wood sandpiper) as well as common passage migrants. Tringa sandpipers are characteristically nervous and alert birds — the redshank in particular functions as a sentinel species in European wetlands, its loud, piping alarm calls instantly alerting every bird in the area to potential predators. Many Tringa species breed in Scandinavia and pass through Europe in large numbers during autumn migration, when estuary mudflats and lake shores can be covered in feeding flocks.

children.name: Tringa totanus
children.description: The common redshank or simply redshank is a Eurasian wader in the large family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Tringa erythropus
children.description: The spotted redshank is a wader (shorebird) in the large bird family Scolopacidae. It breeds across northern Scandinavia and the northern Palearctic and migrates south to the Mediterranean, the southern British Isles, France, tropical Africa, and tropical Asia for the winter. It is an occasional vagrant to Australia and North America.

children.name: Tringa nebularia
children.description: The common greenshank is a wader in the large family Scolopacidae, the typical waders. The genus name Tringa is the Neo-Latin name given to the green sandpiper by Aldrovandus in 1599 based on Ancient Greek trungas, a thrush-sized, white-rumped, tail-bobbing wading bird mentioned by Aristotle. The specific nebularia is from Latin nebula "mist".

children.name: Tringa stagnatilis
children.description: The marsh sandpiper is a small wader. It is a rather small shank, and breeds in open grassy steppe and taiga wetlands from easternmost Europe to the Russian Far East. The genus name Tringa is the Neo-Latin name given to the green sandpiper by Aldrovandus in 1599 based on Ancient Greek trungas, a thrush-sized, white-rumped, tail-bobbing wading bird mentioned by Aristotle.

children.name: Tringa flavipes
children.description: The lesser yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes) is a medium-sized shorebird.

children.name: Tringa melanoleuca
children.description: The greater yellowlegs (Tringa melanoleuca) is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Tringa solitaria
children.description: The solitary sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) is a small shorebird.

children.name: Tringa ochropus
children.description: The green sandpiper is a small wader (shorebird) of the Old World.

children.name: Tringa glareola
children.description: The wood sandpiper is a small wader belonging to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae. A Eurasian species, it is the smallest of the shanks, a genus of mid-sized, long-legged waders that largely inhabit freshwater and wetland environments, as opposed to the maritime or coastal habitats of other, similar species.

children.name: Tringa incana
children.description: The wandering tattler (Tringa incana) is a medium-sized shorebird, similar in appearance to the closely related gray-tailed tattler (T.

children.name: Actitis
children.description: Common sandpiper and spotted sandpiper — two small, distinctive waders defined by their habit of constantly bobbing the rear of their body up and down as they walk. The common sandpiper is one of the most widespread and familiar waders in the Palearctic, found on the banks and shores of virtually every lake, river, and stream. Both species are characterised by a stiff-winged, low flight interspersed with glides on bowed wings just above the water surface. The two species are closely related but have complementary distributions: hypoleucos in the Old World, macularius in the Americas.

children.name: Actitis hypoleucos
children.description: The common sandpiper is a small Palearctic wader. This bird and its American sister species, the spotted sandpiper, make up the genus Actitis. They are parapatric and replace each other geographically; stray birds of either species may settle down with breeders of the other and hybridize.

children.name: Actitis macularius
children.description: The spotted sandpiper is a small shorebird. Together with its sister species the common sandpiper, it makes up the genus Actitis. They replace each other geographically; stray birds may settle down with breeders of the other species and hybridize.

children.name: Calidris
children.description: Stints, sandpipers, and allies — the most diverse genus of small waders, encompassing the majority of the world's diminutive shorebirds and including several larger species such as the knot and the ruff. Calidris species are primarily known as passage migrants and winter visitors to coasts, with a few species breeding in Arctic and subarctic zones. The dunlin is the most abundant small wader on European coasts outside the breeding season; in autumn it forms huge, densely packed flocks that wheel and turn over tidal flats in perfectly synchronised murmurations. Many Calidris species undergo dramatic seasonal plumage changes, appearing strikingly different in breeding and non-breeding seasons.

children.name: Calidris alpina
children.description: The dunlin is a small wader in the genus Calidris. The English name is a dialect form of "dunling", first recorded in 1531–1532. It derives from dun, "dull brown", with the suffix -ling, meaning a person or thing with the given quality.

children.name: Calidris canutus
children.description: The red knot or just knot is a medium-sized shorebird which breeds in tundra and the Arctic Cordillera in the far north of Canada, Europe, and Russia. It is a large member of the Calidris sandpipers, second only to the great knot. Six subspecies are recognised.

children.name: Calidris tenuirostris
children.description: The great knot (Calidris tenuirostris) is a medium-sized wader.

children.name: Calidris alba
children.description: The sanderling is a small wading bird. It is a circumpolar Arctic breeder, being among the most extreme northern breeding birds in the world, nesting only on the coldest tundra, north of the 5°C July isotherm; in Europe, its southernmost breeding locality is Svalbard, where only a handful (5–15) pairs breed. It is a long-distance migrant, wintering south to South America, western and southern Europe, Africa, and Australia.

children.name: Calidris ferruginea
children.description: The curlew sandpiper is a small wader. It is a long-distance migrant, breeding in the bogs and coastal lowlands of the Siberian Arctic, arriving there in June and staying until August or September. After the breeding season, it migrates south to spend the winter in Africa and along the coasts of Oceania and southern Eurasia, occupying tidal mudflats and saltpans.

children.name: Calidris maritima
children.description: The purple sandpiper (Calidris maritima) is a small shorebird in the sandpiper family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Calidris temminckii
children.description: Temminck's stint is a small wader native to the Old World. This bird's common name and Latin binomial commemorate the Dutch naturalist Coenraad Jacob Temminck. The genus name is from Ancient Greek kalidris or skalidris, a term used by Aristotle for some grey-coloured waterside birds.

children.name: Calidris minuta
children.description: The little stint is a very small wader. It breeds in arctic Europe and Asia, and is a long-distance migrant, wintering south to Africa and south Asia. It occasionally is a vagrant to North America and to Australia.

children.name: Calidris minutilla
children.description: The least sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) is the smallest shorebird.

children.name: Calidris pusilla
children.description: The semipalmated sandpiper (Calidris pusilla) is a very small shorebird.

children.name: Calidris mauri
children.description: The western sandpiper (Calidris mauri) is a small migratory shorebird.

children.name: Calidris melanotos
children.description: The pectoral sandpiper, often abbreviated pec, is a small, migratory wader that breeds in arctic regions of North America and Asia, wintering in South America and Oceania. It eats small invertebrates. Its nest, a hole scraped in the ground and with a thick lining, is deep enough to protect its four eggs from the cool breezes of its breeding grounds.

children.name: Calidris himantopus
children.description: The stilt sandpiper (Calidris himantopus) is a small shorebird.

children.name: Calidris falcinellus
children.description: The broad-billed sandpiper is a small wading bird. The scientific specific name falcinellus is the diminutive from Latin falx, falcis, "a small sickle". It was formerly treated in its own monospecific genus Limicola, but this was found to be embedded within the wider genus Calidris, into which it was transferred in 2004.

children.name: Calidris ptilocnemis
children.description: The rock sandpiper (Calidris ptilocnemis) is a small shorebird in the sandpiper family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Calidris subruficollis
children.description: The buff-breasted sandpiper is a small shorebird. The species name subruficollis is from Latin subrufus, "reddish" and collis, "-necked/-throated". It is a calidrid sandpiper.

children.name: Calidris pugnax
children.description: The ruff is a medium-sized wading bird that breeds in marshes and wet meadows across northern Eurasia. This highly gregarious sandpiper is migratory and sometimes forms huge flocks in its winter grounds, which include southern and western Europe, Africa, southern Asia and Australia.

children.name: Arenaria
children.description: Turnstones — two species of stocky, short-billed waders named for their habit of flipping over stones, seaweed, and other debris with rapid sideways movements of the bill to expose small invertebrates sheltering beneath. The ruddy turnstone is one of the most widespread and cosmopolitan waders in the world, wintering on rocky shores on virtually every coastline from the Arctic to the Antarctic. Turnstones are highly adaptable feeders, known to eat carrion, birds' eggs, and even human food when other prey is scarce. The bold black-and-white and chestnut patterning of the breeding plumage ruddy turnstone is one of the most striking of any wader.

children.name: Arenaria interpres
children.description: The ruddy turnstone is a small cosmopolitan wading bird, one of two species of turnstone in the genus Arenaria.

children.name: Arenaria melanocephala
children.description: The black turnstone (Arenaria melanocephala) is a species of small wading bird.

children.name: Phalaropus
children.description: Phalaropes — three remarkable species that are unique among waders in being strongly pelagic outside the breeding season, spending months on the open ocean. They have lobed toes for swimming, and are famous for their reversed sexual roles: females are more brightly coloured than males and compete for mates, while males perform all incubation and chick-rearing duties. Phalaropes feed by spinning rapidly on the water surface, creating a small vortex that draws invertebrates upward. The red-necked phalarope is one of the most abundant and wide-ranging waders in the world, with populations of millions.

children.name: Phalaropus lobatus
children.description: The red-necked phalarope, also known as the northern phalarope and hyperborean phalarope, is a small wader. This phalarope breeds in the Arctic regions of North America and Eurasia. It is migratory, and, unusually for a wader, winters at sea on tropical oceans.

children.name: Phalaropus fulicarius
children.description: The red phalarope or grey phalarope is a small wader. This phalarope breeds in the Arctic regions of North America and Eurasia. It is migratory, and, unusually for a wader, migrates mainly on oceanic routes, wintering at sea on tropical oceans.

children.name: Limnodromus
children.description: Dowitchers — three species of medium-sized, long-billed waders named for their distinctive feeding action of plunging the bill vertically into soft mud in rapid, repeated sewing-machine motions. They combine the elongated bill of a snipe with a plump body and medium-length legs. The two North American species, long-billed and short-billed dowitchers, are among the most challenging identification problems in shorebird watching, being nearly identical in appearance but separable by call. The Asian dowitcher is the most range-restricted of the three, breeding in central Asia and migrating to Southeast Asia.

children.name: Limnodromus scolopaceus
children.description: The long-billed dowitcher is a medium-sized shorebird with a relatively long bill belonging to the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae. In breeding plumage, adults are characterized by a rufous head and underparts with a darker mottled back and a large white upper rump only seen in flight. They feed in various freshwater habitats with their bill underwater in a "sewing machine" motion and have a mating display where males chase females in flight.

children.name: Limnodromus semipalmatus
children.description: thumb|300px|left|Video at Manly Marina, [[South East Queensland]].

children.name: Xenus
children.description: Terek sandpiper — a monotypic genus containing a single distinctive species characterised by its strongly upturned bill and remarkable forward-tilting feeding posture. The terek sandpiper is one of the most active and energetic of all waders, running rapidly along mudflats with its body tilted forward and bill angled upward, in pursuit of fiddler crabs and other small invertebrates. Its name Xenus means 'stranger' or 'alien' in Greek, referring to its unusual bill shape. Despite its odd morphology it is clearly part of the Tringa–Actitis clade within the Scolopacidae.

children.name: Xenus cinereus
children.description: The Terek sandpiper (Xenus cinereus) is a small migratory Palearctic wader species and is the only member of the genus Xenus.

children.name: Bartramia
children.description: Upland sandpiper — a monotypic genus containing one of the most distinctive of all shorebirds, notable for its preference for dry upland grasslands rather than wetlands, its small dove-like head on a long neck, and its haunting, liquid whistling calls. Named after John Bartram, the pioneering American botanist. The upland sandpiper is one of the most important migratory landbirds of the North American interior, undertaking a remarkable migration between its grassland breeding grounds and the South American pampas.

children.name: Bartramia longicauda
children.description: The upland sandpiper (Bartramia longicauda) is a large sandpiper, closely related to the curlews.

children.name: Tryngites
children.description: Buff-breasted sandpiper — a monotypic genus (now often included within Calidris) containing a single distinctive sandpiper of dry tundra and grasslands. Sometimes treated as part of Calidris based on molecular phylogenetics, but retained here as a traditional genus. The species is famous for its extraordinary lek display behaviour and for the dramatic sexual dimorphism in size — males considerably larger than females. A bird of open landscapes, it breeds on dry Arctic tundra and winters on the pampas of South America.

children.name: Prosobonia
children.description: Pacific sandpipers — a genus of enigmatic small sandpipers restricted to remote Pacific islands, representing the outcome of ancient colonisation events from the wider Scolopacidae. Two living species are recognised, both found in the Tuamotu and Kiribati archipelagos; additional species are known from fossil records on other Pacific islands. These birds evolved in isolation on oceanic atolls, developing adaptations for foraging in coral reef and beach environments far from the continental wetland habitats typical of most scolopacids.

children.name: Prosobonia cancellata
children.description: The Christmas sandpiper or Kiritimati sandpiper (Prosobonia cancellata) is an extinct species of small shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.

children.name: Prosobonia ellisi
children.description: The Moorea sandpiper (Prosobonia ellisi) is an extinct member of the large wader family Scolopacidae that was endemic to Mo'orea in French Polynesia, where the locals called it te-te in the Tahitian language.

children.name: Alca
children.description: Razorbills — medium-sized auks of the North Atlantic, named for the distinctive laterally compressed bill that is crossed with a white line. The razorbill (tordmule) is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk and shares its stocky, black-and-white coloration and awkward gait on land. In Sweden, razorbills breed on rocky sea cliffs on the west coast, particularly on Stora Karlsö off Gotland and at Nidingen on the Kattegat. Like all auks, razorbills are consummate underwater fliers, using their wings to pursue fish at depth. They are highly colonial breeders, choosing crevices and ledges in cliff faces rather than the open ledges preferred by guillemots.

children.name: Alca torda
children.description: The razorbill is a North Atlantic colonial seabird and the only extant member of the genus Alca of the family Alcidae, the auks. It is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk. Historically, it has also been known as "auk", "razor-billed auk" and "lesser auk".

children.name: Uria
children.description: Guillemots — the most abundant large seabirds in the North Atlantic, nesting in enormous cliff colonies that can contain hundreds of thousands of birds. The common guillemot (sillgrissla) breeds in one of the densest aggregations of any bird: pairs share tiny cliff ledges so tightly that incubating birds are pressed shoulder to shoulder in ranks, exchanging constant mutual preening and loud guttural calls. Guillemots lay a single pear-shaped egg directly on the bare rock — the tapering shape means it rolls in a tight circle rather than off the ledge. Chicks jump from the colony to the sea before they can fly, at around three weeks old, and are tended at sea by the father. Sweden's guillemot colonies, concentrated on limestone stacks off Gotland and the Kattegat archipelago, are among the most important seabird sites in the Baltic region.

children.name: Uria aalge
children.description: The common murre or common guillemot is a large auk, one of several species called murre or guillemot. It has a circumpolar distribution, occurring in low-Arctic and boreal waters in the North Atlantic and North Pacific. It spends most of its time at sea, only coming to land to breed on rocky cliff shores or islands.

children.name: Cepphus
children.description: Black guillemots — smaller, rounder auks that differ fundamentally from their relatives in breeding close inshore, in small dispersed groups rather than large colonies, and in remaining in their breeding areas year-round rather than migrating to open ocean. The black guillemot (tobisgrissla) is one of the most characteristic birds of the Swedish outer archipelago, breeding under boulders and in rock crevices on skerry islands throughout the Baltic and Kattegat coasts. In breeding plumage it is entirely jet black with a large white wing patch and vivid scarlet feet and gape — one of the most striking of all Swedish seabirds. Its piping calls are a defining sound of the Swedish summer archipelago. Unlike other auks it dives primarily for bottom-dwelling fish and invertebrates in relatively shallow coastal waters.

children.name: Cepphus columba
children.description: The pigeon guillemot (Cepphus columba) ( ) is a species of bird in the auk family, Alcidae.

children.name: Cepphus carbo
children.description: The spectacled guillemot or sooty guillemot (Cepphus carbo) is a seabird in the auk family.

children.name: Alle
children.description: Little auk — the smallest North Atlantic auk, barely larger than a starling yet one of the most abundant seabirds in the world, with breeding colonies in the High Arctic (particularly northwestern Greenland and Svalbard) numbering in the millions. The little auk (alkekung) is a highly pelagic bird, spending its non-breeding months far out in the North Atlantic and Barents Sea where it feeds on copepods and other tiny crustaceans. It very rarely approaches Swedish coasts voluntarily, but in years of severe autumn storms, exhausted and disoriented birds may be blown inland — 'wrecks' of little auks occasionally occur in Sweden when Atlantic gales sweep birds far from their usual pelagic range.

children.name: Alle alle
children.description: The little auk (Europe) or dovekie (North America) (Alle alle) is a small auk, the only member of the genus Alle.

children.name: Fratercula
children.description: Puffins — the most iconic and instantly recognisable of all the auks, beloved for their clown-like colourful bill and upright posture. The Atlantic puffin (lunnefågel) breeds in burrows excavated in soft coastal turf on offshore islands. In Sweden, the main breeding sites are on Nidingen and Hallands Väderö off the Kattegat coast — the easternmost significant puffin colonies in Europe. Sweden's puffin population is small and has declined sharply since the mid-20th century, making each individual a precious sight. Puffins carry multiple sand eels crosswise in the bill simultaneously (using backward-facing serrations to hold earlier catches while catching more) — some individuals have been recorded carrying over 60 fish in a single bill-load.

children.name: Fratercula arctica
children.description: The Atlantic puffin, also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family. It is the only puffin native to the Atlantic Ocean; two related species, the tufted puffin and the horned puffin, are found in the northeastern Pacific. The Atlantic puffin breeds in Russia, Iceland, Ireland, Britain, Norway, Greenland, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and the Faroe Islands, and as far south as Maine in the west and France in the east.

children.name: Fratercula cirrhata
children.description: The tufted puffin (Fratercula cirrhata), also known as crested puffin, is a relatively abundant medium-sized pelagic seabird in the auk family (Alcidae) found throughout the North Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Fratercula corniculata
children.description: The horned puffin (Fratercula corniculata) is an auk found in the North Pacific Ocean, including the coasts of Alaska, Siberia and British Columbia.

children.name: Brachyramphus
children.description: Murrelets of the North Pacific — small, cryptically patterned auks with a unique nesting habit: they do not breed in colonies but lay eggs singly on the mossy branches of old-growth trees or on remote alpine scree, far from the sea. The Marbled Murrelet's dependence on coastal old-growth forest has made it a flagship species for Pacific Northwest forest conservation.

children.name: Brachyramphus marmoratus
children.description: The marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus) is a small seabird from the North Pacific.

children.name: Synthliboramphus
children.description: The ancient murrelets of the North Pacific — small auks that fly from the colony to the open ocean within days of hatching, never returning to land until they breed. They are the most precocial of all seabirds: chicks jump from the nest on the second night after hatching and follow their parents out to sea, swimming and diving from the first moment.

children.name: Synthliboramphus antiquus
children.description: The ancient murrelet () is a bird in the auk family.

children.name: Synthliboramphus hypoleucus
children.description: The Guadalupe murrelet (Synthliboramphus hypoleucus) or Xantus's murrelet is a small seabird found in the California Current system in the Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Ptychoramphus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing Cassin's Auklet — a small, stubby-billed auklet of the North Pacific that is one of the most abundant seabirds on the California Current system. It nests in burrows on offshore islands and is an important indicator of ocean health for fisheries management.

children.name: Aethia
children.description: The four smallest auklets — tiny seabirds of the North Pacific that breed in immense colonies on volcanic islands, often alongside each other. They are adorned with a remarkable array of facial plumes and horny plates used in courtship displays. The Least Auklet at 85 g is the smallest of all alcids, while the Crested Auklet has a forward-curving forehead crest and produces a strong citrus-like scent during the breeding season.

children.name: Aethia psittacula
children.description: The parakeet auklet (Aethia psittacula) is a small seabird of the North Pacific.

children.name: Aethia pusilla
children.description: The least auklet (Aethia pusilla) is a seabird and the smallest species of auk.

children.name: Aethia pygmaea
children.description: The whiskered auklet is a small seabird of the auk family. It has a more restricted range than other members of its genus, Aethia, living only around the Aleutian Islands and on some islands off Siberia, and breeding on these islands. It is one of the smallest alcids, only the closely related least auklet being smaller.

children.name: Aethia cristatella
children.description: The crested auklet is a small seabird of the family Alcidae, distributed throughout the northern Pacific and the Bering Sea. The species feeds by diving in deep waters, eating krill and a variety of small marine animals. It nests in dense colonies of up to 1 million individuals in the Bering Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk.

children.name: Cerorhinca
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Rhinoceros Auklet — a puffin-like auk that is the closest living relative of the puffins. It is named for the horny 'rhinoceros-like' projection at the base of the bill in breeding season. Despite its name it is larger and heavier than any true auklet, approaching the size of a small puffin.

children.name: Cerorhinca monocerata
children.description: The rhinoceros auklet (Cerorhinca monocerata) is a seabird and a close relative of the puffins.

children.name: Pinguinus
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Great Auk — the largest of all auks and the only one entirely flightless, rendered vulnerable by its inability to fly and ruthlessly exterminated by 19th-century hunters for its feathers, meat, and oil. The last breeding pair was killed on Eldey Island, Iceland, in 1844, and the last confirmed individual was seen on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland in 1852. The Great Auk is one of the most iconic species extinctions of the modern era.

children.name: Pinguinus impennis
children.description: The great auk (Pinguinus impennis), also known as the garefowl or penguin, is an extinct species of flightless alcid that first appeared around 400,000 years ago and was driven to extinction by human exploitation in the mid-19th century.

children.name: Pluvialis
children.description: Large upright plovers of open habitats. The mournful whistle of the Golden Plover is the defining sound of Swedish upland mires and heaths; autumn flocks of tens of thousands gather on coastal farmland.

children.name: Pluvialis apricaria
children.description: The European golden plover, also known as the Eurasian golden plover, greater golden plover, or just the golden plover within Europe, is a relatively large species of plover. This species is similar to two other golden plovers, the American golden plover, Pluvialis dominica, and Pacific golden plover, Pluvialis fulva, which are both slightly smaller, slimmer and longer-legged than European golden plover, and both have grey rather than white axillary (armpit) feathers.

children.name: Pluvialis squatarola
children.description: The grey plover or black-bellied plover is a large plover breeding in Arctic regions. It is a long-distance migrant, with a nearly worldwide coastal distribution when not breeding.

children.name: Pluvialis fulva
children.description: The Pacific golden plover is a migratory shorebird that breeds during summer in Alaska and Siberia. During nonbreeding season, this medium-sized plover migrates widely across the Pacific.

children.name: Pluvialis dominica
children.description: The American golden plover (Pluvialis dominica) is a medium-sized plover.

children.name: Oreopholus
children.description: A monotypic genus of high-altitude South American plover.

children.name: Hoploxypterus
children.description: A monotypic South American genus, the pied plover is sometimes placed in Vanellus but differs in plumage and structure.

children.name: Hoploxypterus cayanus
children.description: | range_map = Hoploxypterus cayanus map.svg.

children.name: Phegornis
children.description: A monotypic Andean genus with a uniquely long, slender bill for probing among rocks.

children.name: Zonibyx
children.description: A monotypic genus for the rufous-chested dotterel of southern South America, placed here based on molecular phylogenetic evidence.

children.name: Eudromias
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Eurasian Dotterel, separated from Charadrius on genetic grounds. The male alone incubates and cares for the young.

children.name: Eudromias morinellus
children.description: The Eurasian dotterel (Eudromias morinellus), also known in Europe as just dotterel, is a small wader in the plover family of birds.

children.name: Charadrius
children.description: Core ringed-plover genus, now restricted to four species after the transfer of many species to Anarhynchus and Thinornis based on molecular phylogenetics.

children.name: Charadrius hiaticula
children.description: The common ringed plover, great ringed plover or ringed plover is a species of bird in the family Charadriidae. It breeds across much of northern Eurasia, as well as Greenland.

children.name: Charadrius semipalmatus
children.description: The semipalmated plover (Charadrius semipalmatus) is a small plover.

children.name: Charadrius melodus
children.description: The piping plover (Charadrius melodus) is a sand-colored, sparrow-sized shorebird that nests and feeds along coastal sand and gravel beaches in North America.

children.name: Charadrius dubius
children.description: The little ringed plover is a small plover native to the Old World. It has mostly brown upperparts, a black neckband and a black mask around the eye with a noticeable yellow eyering. Its forehead, belly and the rest of the breast are white.

children.name: Charadrius collaris
children.description: The collared plover (Anarhynchus collaris) is a small shorebird in the plover family, Charadriidae.

children.name: Thinornis
children.description: A genus of plovers expanded by molecular studies to include the little ringed plover and several Southern Hemisphere species formerly placed in Charadrius.

children.name: Thinornis cucullatus
children.description: The hooded plover or hooded dotterel (Thinornis cucullatus) is a species of bird in the family Charadriidae.

children.name: Thinornis novaeseelandiae
children.description: The shore plover (, Moriori: , Thinornis novaeseelandiae), also known as the shore dotterel, is a small plover endemic to New Zealand.

children.name: Elseyornis
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Black-fronted Dotterel, a small, boldly patterned plover of Australian and New Zealand watercourses with a distinctive black breast-band and chestnut back-patch.

children.name: Vanellus
children.description: Lapwings with broad rounded wings, elaborate crests and often facial wattles or carpal spurs. Found on every continent except Antarctica.

children.name: Vanellus vanellus
children.description: The northern lapwing, also known as the peewit or pewit, tuit or tewit, green plover, or pyewipe or just lapwing, is a bird in the lapwing subfamily. It is common through temperate Eurosiberia.

children.name: Vanellus armatus
children.description: The blacksmith lapwing or blacksmith plover (Vanellus armatus) is a lapwing species that occurs commonly from Kenya through central Tanzania to southern and southwestern Africa.

children.name: Vanellus duvaucelii
children.description: The river lapwing (Vanellus duvaucelii) is a lapwing species which breeds from the Indian subcontinent eastwards to Southeast Asia.

children.name: Vanellus lugubris
children.description: :The African wattled lapwing (Vanellus senegallus) is sometimes called Senegal wattled plover.

children.name: Vanellus coronatus
children.description: The crowned lapwing (Vanellus coronatus), or crowned plover, is a bird of the lapwing subfamily that occurs contiguously from the Red Sea coast of Somalia to southern and southwestern Africa.

children.name: Vanellus senegallus
children.description: The African wattled lapwing (Vanellus senegallus), also known as the Senegal wattled plover or simply wattled lapwing, is a large lapwing, a group of largish waders in the family Charadriidae.

children.name: Vanellus macropterus
children.description: The Javan lapwing (Vanellus macropterus) also known as Javanese lapwing and Javanese wattled lapwing is a wader in the lapwing family.

children.name: Vanellus tricolor
children.description: The banded lapwing (Vanellus tricolor) is a small to medium-sized shorebird, found in small parties or large flocks on bare ground in open grasslands, agricultural land and open savannah.

children.name: Vanellus miles
children.description: The masked lapwing (Vanellus miles) is a large, common and conspicuous bird native to Australia (particularly the northern and eastern parts of the continent), New Zealand and New Guinea.

children.name: Vanellus gregarius
children.description: The sociable lapwing (Vanellus gregarius), referred to as the sociable plover in the UK, is a wader in the plover family.

children.name: Vanellus chilensis
children.description: thumb|Southern Lapwing observed in Indaiatuba, SP, Brazil.

children.name: Vanellus resplendens
children.description: The Andean lapwing (Vanellus resplendens) is a species of bird in family Charadriidae, the plovers and their relatives.

children.name: Erythrogonys
children.description: A monotypic genus distinguished by its red legs and unique plumage pattern among Charadriidae.

children.name: Peltohyas
children.description: A monotypic genus superbly camouflaged for Australia's arid interior; formerly thought to be related to coursers.

children.name: Peltohyas australis
children.description: The inland dotterel or inland plover (Peltohyas australis) is an endemic bird of the arid Australian interior.

children.name: Anarhynchus
children.description: A large genus of plovers greatly expanded after molecular studies confirmed that many Charadrius species are more closely related to the wrybill. Characterised by partial collars rather than full breast bands.

children.name: Anarhynchus veredus
children.description: The oriental plover (Anarhynchus veredus), also known as the oriental dotterel, is a medium-sized plover closely related to the Caspian plover.

children.name: Anarhynchus mongolus
children.description: The Siberian sand plover (Anarhynchus mongolus) is a small wader in the plover family of birds.

children.name: Anarhynchus leschenaultii
children.description: The greater sand plover (Anarhynchus leschenaultii) is a small wader in the plover family of birds.

children.name: Anarhynchus collaris
children.description: The collared plover (Anarhynchus collaris) is a small shorebird in the plover family, Charadriidae.

children.name: Anarhynchus montanus
children.description: The mountain plover (Anarhynchus montanus) is a medium-sized ground bird in the plover family (Charadriidae).

children.name: Anarhynchus alticola
children.description: The puna plover (Anarhynchus alticola) is a species of bird in subfamily Charadriinae of family Charadriidae.

children.name: Anarhynchus thoracicus
children.description: The Madagascar plover (Anarhynchus thoracicus), also known as the black-banded plover, is a small (37 g) monogamous shorebird in the family Charadriidae, native to western Madagascar.

children.name: Anarhynchus nivosus
children.description: The snowy plover (Anarhynchus nivosus, formerly Charadrius nivosus) is a small shorebird found in the Americas.

children.name: Anarhynchus peronii
children.description: The Malaysian plover or Malay plover (Anarhynchus peronii, syn.

children.name: Anarhynchus javanicus
children.description: The Javan plover (Anarhynchus javanicus) is a Charadriidae species with an unclear taxonomic status.

children.name: Anarhynchus alexandrinus
children.description: The Kentish plover (Anarhynchus alexandrinus) is a small wader () of the family Charadriidae that breeds on the shores of saline lakes, lagoons, and coasts, populating sand dunes, marshes, semi-arid desert, and tundra.

children.name: Haematopus
children.description: Noisy pied waders of rocky shores. The bright orange bill is used to prise open mussels or stab open cockles — each individual learns one technique and uses it for life. Their loud piping calls are a defining sound of the Swedish archipelago coastline.

children.name: Haematopus ostralegus
children.description: The Eurasian oystercatcher or European oystercatcher, also known as the common pied oystercatcher, or just oystercatcher, is a wader in the oystercatcher bird family Haematopodidae. It has striking black and white plumage, a long straight orange-red bill, red eyes and relatively short dull pink legs. The sexes are similar in appearance but the bill of the female is longer than that of the male.

children.name: Haematopus palliatus
children.description: The American oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus), occasionally called the American pied oystercatcher, is a member of family Haematopodidae.

children.name: Haematopus bachmani
children.description: The black oystercatcher (Haematopus bachmani) is a conspicuous black bird found on the shoreline of western North America, ranging from the Aleutian Islands of Alaska to the coast of the Baja California peninsula.

children.name: Haematopus moquini
children.description: The African oystercatcher or African black oystercatcher (Haematopus moquini) is a large charismatic wader resident to the mainland coasts and offshore islands of southern Africa.

children.name: Haematopus fuliginosus
children.description: The sooty oystercatcher (Haematopus fuliginosus) is a species of oystercatcher.

children.name: Haematopus longirostris
children.description: The pied oystercatcher (Haematopus longirostris) is a species of oystercatcher.

children.name: Haematopus unicolor
children.description: The variable oystercatcher is a species of wader in the family Haematopodidae. It is endemic to New Zealand. The Māori name is tōrea-pango.

children.name: Haematopus finschi
children.description: The South Island oystercatcher or South Island pied oystercatcher is one of two common oystercatcher species found in New Zealand. Its name is often contracted to the acronym "SIPO". The indigenous Māori name is tōrea.

children.name: Haematopus leucopodus
children.description: The Magellanic oystercatcher (Haematopus leucopodus) is a species of wader in the family Haematopodidae.

children.name: Haematopus ophthalmicus
children.description: The eastern far-eastern populations of the oystercatcher complex breeding in Kamchatka and northeast Asia, sometimes treated as a distinct race, with a very prominent orange eye-ring. Coastal and estuarine.

children.name: Recurvirostra
children.description: Elegant pied waders with distinctively upturned bills swept through shallow water to catch invertebrates. The Pied Avocet breeds in shallow saline lagoons in southern Sweden — Öland and Gotland — and is expanding northward.

children.name: Recurvirostra avosetta
children.description: The pied avocet is a species of wader in the Recurvirostridae family, the only member of the avocet genus Recurvirostra found in Europe, Africa, and Asia.

children.name: Recurvirostra americana
children.description: The American avocet (Recurvirostra americana) is a large wader in the avocet and stilt family, Recurvirostridae, found in North America.

children.name: Recurvirostra andina
children.description: | range_map = Recurvirostra andina map.svg.

children.name: Himantopus
children.description: Extravagantly long-legged black-and-white waders.

children.name: Himantopus himantopus
children.description: The black-winged stilt is a widely distributed, very long-legged wader in the avocet and stilt family Recurvirostridae. Its scientific name, Himantopus himantopus, is sometimes used to generalize a single, almost cosmopolitan species. Alternatively, it is restricted to the form that is widespread in Europe, Asia and Africa, which equals the nominate group of H.
