children.name: Himantopus mexicanus
children.description: The black-necked stilt, also called the pied stilt, is a locally abundant shorebird of North and South American wetlands and coastlines. It is found from the coastal areas of California through much of the interior western United States and along the Gulf of Mexico as far east as Florida, then south through Central America and the Caribbean to Brazil, Peru and the Galápagos Islands, with an isolated population, the Hawaiian stilt, in Hawaii. The northernmost populations, particularly those from inland, are migratory, wintering from the extreme south of the United States to southern Mexico, rarely as far south as Costa Rica; on the Baja California peninsula it is only found regularly in winter.

children.name: Himantopus leucocephalus
children.description: The pied stilt (Himantopus leucocephalus), also known as the white-headed stilt, is a shorebird in the family Recurvirostridae.

children.name: Himantopus novaezelandiae
children.description: The black stilt or kakī (Māori), (Himantopus novaezelandiae) is a wading bird found in New Zealand.

children.name: Cladorhynchus
children.description: A monotypic genus of nomadic Australian wader that breeds explosively on ephemeral inland salt lakes.

children.name: Cladorhynchus leucocephalus
children.description: The banded stilt (Cladorhynchus leucocephalus) is a nomadic wader of the stilt and avocet family, Recurvirostridae, native to Australia.

children.name: Ibidorhyncha
children.description: A distinctive monotypic Asian wader of high mountain rivers, sometimes placed in its own family.

children.name: Stercorarius
children.description: Piratical seabirds that relentlessly pursue other birds until they drop or disgorge their food. The Long-tailed Skua breeds on Swedish mountain tundra; the others are passage migrants offshore. Dark and pale morphs occur in several species.

children.name: Stercorarius parasiticus
children.description: The parasitic jaeger or arctic skua, also known as the parasitic skua or arctic jaeger, is a seabird in the skua family Stercorariidae. It is a migratory species breeding in Northern Fennoscandia, Scotland, Iceland, Greenland, Northern Canada, Alaska, and Siberia and wintering across the southern hemisphere. Kleptoparasitism is a major source of food for this species during migration and winter, and is where the name is derived from.

children.name: Stercorarius pomarinus
children.description: The pomarine jaeger, pomarine skua, or pomatorhine skua, is a seabird in the skua family Stercorariidae. It is a migrant, wintering at sea in the tropical oceans.

children.name: Stercorarius longicaudus
children.description: The long-tailed jaeger or long-tailed skua is a seabird in the skua family Stercorariidae.

children.name: Stercorarius skua
children.description: The great skua (Stercorarius skua), sometimes known by the name bonxie in Britain, is a large seabird in the skua family Stercorariidae.

children.name: Stercorarius antarcticus
children.description: | range_map = Catharacta antarctica map.svg.

children.name: Stercorarius maccormicki
children.description: The south polar skua (Stercorarius maccormicki) is a large seabird in the skua family, Stercorariidae.

children.name: Stercorarius chilensis
children.description: The Chilean skua, also known as the cinnamon skua (Stercorarius chilensis), is a large predatory seabird, which breeds in Argentina and Chile, but ranges as far north as Brazil and Peru when not breeding.

children.name: Burhinus
children.description: Thick-knees — nocturnal waders named for their prominent, swollen-looking knee joints (actually the ankle). Their large yellow eyes have excellent night vision, allowing them to hunt insects and small vertebrates under cover of darkness. By day they rely on their cryptic plumage to remain invisible against stones and dry earth. Their haunting, wailing calls at dusk are characteristic of open stony landscapes.

children.name: Burhinus oedicnemus
children.description: The Eurasian stone-curlew, Eurasian thick-knee, or simply stone-curlew (Burhinus oedicnemus) is a northern species of the Burhinidae (stone-curlew) bird family.

children.name: Burhinus senegalensis
children.description: The Senegal thick-knee (Burhinus senegalensis) is a stone-curlew, a group of waders in the family Burhinidae.

children.name: Burhinus grallarius
children.description: The bush stone-curlew or bush thick-knee (Burhinus grallarius, obsolete name Burhinus magnirostris) is a large, ground-dwelling bird endemic to Australia.

children.name: Burhinus alticola
children.description: Found in arid regions, the Alticola Stone-curve is a ground-dwelling bird with distinctive grey and white plumage. It breeds in rocky outcrops and grasslands.

children.name: Esacus tibetanus
children.description: The Tibetan Thick-knee is a well adapted bird to the harsh, high-altitude environment of the Tibetan Plateau. It has thick, grey feathers and a distinctive call.

children.name: Amaurornis australis
children.description: The Southern Thick-knee is a large, ground-dwelling bird with a distinctive call. It breeds in open grasslands and rocky outcrops.

children.name: Esacus
children.description: Large, heavy-bodied stone-curlews with massive, brightly coloured bills. They inhabit coastal shorelines and large rivers, where their powerful bills are used to crush hard-shelled crabs and molluscs. They are more diurnal than Burhinus thick-knees and are found from Africa through South Asia to Australia.

children.name: Esacus recurvirostris
children.description: The great stone-curlew or great thick-knee (Esacus recurvirostris) is a large wader which is a resident breeder in tropical southern Asia from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh into South-east Asia.

children.name: Esacus magnirostris
children.description: The beach stone-curlew (Esacus magnirostris) also known as beach thick-knee is a large, ground-dwelling bird that occurs in Australasia, the islands of South-east Asia.

children.name: Glareola
children.description: Pratincoles — elegant, tern-like waders with long pointed wings and a forked tail. They catch insects on the wing like swallows, flying with a buoyant, swooping action. Their short legs reflect their aerial lifestyle. Nests on open ground in dry plains and salt pans.

children.name: Glareola pratincola
children.description: The collared pratincole (Glareola pratincola), also known as the common pratincole or red-winged pratincole, is a wader in the pratincole family, Glareolidae.

children.name: Glareola maldivarum
children.description: thumb|Glareola maldivarum - Oriental Pratincole.

children.name: Glareola ocularis
children.description: The Madagascar pratincole (Glareola ocularis) is a species of bird in the family Glareolidae.

children.name: Glareola lactea
children.description: The small pratincole, little pratincole, or small Indian pratincole (Glareola lactea) is a small wader in the pratincole family, Glareolidae.

children.name: Glareola nuchalis
children.description: The rock pratincole (Glareola nuchalis) is a species of bird in the family Glareolidae.

children.name: Glareola cinerea
children.description: The grey pratincole (Glareola cinerea) is a species of bird, in the family Glareolidae.

children.name: Tetraonax maxima
children.description: This large pratincole is a spectacular sight in flight, with striking plumage and acrobatic displays during courtship.

children.name: Cathacus alticola
children.description: The Highland Pratincole is a resilient species that inhabits rugged mountainous regions, where it feeds on invertebrates and seeds.

children.name: Cursorius
children.description: Coursers — fast-running waders of arid plains, named for their speed across the ground. Unlike pratincoles, they rarely fly and prefer to run from danger, relying on their superb camouflage. Their elongated hind claws provide stability on loose sand. Found across Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia.

children.name: Cursorius coromandelicus
children.description: The Indian courser (Cursorius coromandelicus) is a species of courser found in mainland South Asia, mainly in the plains bounded by the Ganges and Indus river system.

children.name: Sphenocichla intermedia
children.description: These courser species are swift runners, adept at dashing across open plains and savannas, often seen near termite mounds.

children.name: Rhinoptilus
children.description: Coursers with more heavily patterned plumage than Cursorius, often with bold facial markings and striking wing patterns. They are named for their distinctive nostril structure and are found in the drier regions of Africa and South Asia.

children.name: Jacana
children.description: A genus of two tropical jacana species found in the Americas, known for their elaborate facial wattles and frontal shields. Like all jacanas, they have extraordinarily long toes and claws that allow them to walk across floating vegetation, a behaviour that earned them the colloquial name 'lily-trotters'.

children.name: Jacana spinosa
children.description: The northern jacana or northern jaçana (Jacana spinosa) is a wader which is known as a resident breeder from coastal Mexico to western Panama, and on Cuba, Jamaica and Hispaniola in the Caribbean.

children.name: Jacana jacana
children.description: The wattled jacana (Jacana jacana) is a wader in the family Jacanidae found throughout much of South America east of the Andes, as well as western Panama and Trinidad.

children.name: Actophilornis
children.description: A genus of two African jacanas distinguished by a bright blue bill and frontal shield, with rich chestnut plumage and white underparts. They inhabit freshwater wetlands across the continent and on Madagascar, employing the same reverse sex-role polyandry as other jacanas.

children.name: Actophilornis africanus
children.description: The African jacana (Actophilornis africanus) is a wader in the family Jacanidae.

children.name: Actophilornis albinucha
children.description: The Madagascar jacana (Actophilornis albinucha) is a species of bird in the family Jacanidae.

children.name: Irediparra
children.description: A monotypic genus of the Australasian region, with a distinctive bright red fleshy comb-like wattle covering the forehead and crown. The comb-crested jacana is the only jacana found in both Australia and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Hydrophasianus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the pheasant-tailed jacana, the largest and most elegant member of the family. Unlike other jacanas, this species undergoes a dramatic seasonal plumage change and is a long-distance migratory bird across South and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Microparra
children.description: A monotypic genus of African jacana, the smallest member of the family. The Lesser Jacana is a dainty, delicate bird with a much shorter bill and toes than other jacanas, reflecting its more terrestrial habit and preference for densely vegetated marshes.

children.name: Microparra capensis
children.description: The lesser jacana (Microparra capensis) is a wader in the family Jacanidae and can be found in Africa.

children.name: Metopidius
children.description: A monotypic genus of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, characterised by a bronze-olive back and a prominent white supercilium. The bronze-winged jacana is a common resident of lowland wetlands from Pakistan to Vietnam.

children.name: Ortyxelos
children.description: Ortyxelos — a genus of buttonquail in the family Turnicidae.

children.name: Ortyxelos meiffrenii
children.description: The quail-plover, lark buttonquail or lark-plover is a small ground-living bird in the buttonquail family Turnicidae that is found in the Sahel region of Africa and in a disjunct region of East Africa. It is the only species placed in the genus Ortyxelos.

children.name: Pedionomus
children.description: A monotypic genus now often placed in its own family Pedionomidae, the Plains-wanderer resembles a buttonquail but is genetically distinct. It is one of Australia's most evolutionarily distinctive bird lineages, with no close living relatives.

children.name: Turnix
children.description: Small, cryptically coloured ground birds that resemble true quail but belong to an entirely different order. Buttonquail are unique among birds in that the females are larger and more brightly coloured than males, and they compete for male mates. The males incubate the eggs and raise the young entirely unaided.

children.name: Turnix sylvaticus
children.description: The common buttonquail (Turnix sylvaticus), also called Kurrichane buttonquail and Andalusian hemipode, is a buttonquail, one of a small family of birds that resemble but are not closely related to the true quails.

children.name: Turnix suscitator
children.description: The barred buttonquail or common bustard-quail (Turnix suscitator) is a buttonquail, one of a small family of birds which resemble, but are not closely related to, the true quails.

children.name: Turnix varius
children.description: The painted buttonquail (Turnix varius) is a species of buttonquail, the family Turnicidae, which resemble, but are unrelated to, the quails of Phasianidae.

children.name: Turnix everetti
children.description: The Sumba buttonquail (Turnix everetti) is a species of bird in the family Turnicidae.

children.name: Turnix hottentottus
children.description: The Fynbos buttonquail (Turnix hottentottus) is a bird in the family Turnicidae formerly considered conspecific with the black-rumped buttonquail (Turnix nanus).

children.name: Turnix nigricans
children.description: A buttonquail endemic to Madagascar.

children.name: Turnix velox
children.description: The little buttonquail (Turnix velox) is a species of buttonquail, part of a small family of birds which resemble, but are unrelated to, the true quails.

children.name: Turnix worcesteri
children.description: The Luzon buttonquail (Turnix worcesteri) or Worcester's buttonquail, is a species of bird in the family Turnicidae.

children.name: Turnix ocellatus
children.description: The spotted buttonquail (Turnix ocellatus) is a species of bird in the family Turnicidae.

children.name: Turnix dussumieri
children.description: A buttonquail found in South and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Chionis
children.description: The only Antarctic bird family without webbed feet, sheathbills are stout, pigeon-like shorebirds named for the horny sheath covering the base of their bill. They are opportunistic scavengers that follow penguin colonies and seal haul-outs, feeding on eggs, carrion, and any organic debris. Their white plumage provides camouflage against the snow and ice of their harsh sub-Antarctic and Antarctic home.

children.name: Chionis albus
children.description: The snowy sheathbill (Chionis albus), also known as the greater sheathbill, pale-faced sheathbill, and paddy, is one of two species of sheathbill.

children.name: Pluvianellus
children.description: A monotypic genus of enigmatic shorebird endemic to southern South America. The Magellanic Plover was long placed in the plover family Charadriidae but molecular studies confirm it is distinct enough to warrant its own family. It resembles a pale grey plover with a short, thick bill and red legs.

children.name: Pluvianellus socialis
children.description: The Magellanic plover (Pluvianellus socialis) is a rare wader endemic to southernmost South America.

children.name: Ibidorhyncha
children.description: A monotypic genus instantly recognisable by its long, downward-curved red bill, which it uses to probe under stones in shallow mountain streams. The Ibisbill is a highly specialised shorebird of the high-altitude rivers of Central Asia, straddling the ecological niche between an ibis and a plover.

children.name: Pluvianus
children.description: A monotypic genus of striking wader once placed in the pratincole family Glareolidae but now recognised as a distinct evolutionary lineage. The Egyptian Plover is famous for its supposed symbiotic relationship with crocodiles, cleaning parasites from their mouths — a behaviour documented by Herodotus but rarely observed in modern times.

children.description: ]] The Egyptian plover (Pluvianus aegyptius), also known as the crocodile bird, is a wader, the only member of the genus Pluvianus.

children.name: Rostratula
children.description: Medium-sized waders with beautifully patterned plumage that resembles true snipes but with a noticeably thicker, shorter bill. Like buttonquail, painted-snipes exhibit reversed sexual dimorphism — females are larger and more brightly coloured, competing for males who handle all incubation and chick-rearing. They are secretive marsh-dwellers, more often heard than seen.

children.name: Rostratula benghalensis
children.description: The greater painted-snipe (Rostratula benghalensis) is a species of wader in the small painted-snipe family Rostratulidae.

children.name: Pedionomus
children.description: A monotypic genus representing one of Australia's most evolutionarily distinctive bird lineages. The Plains-wanderer was long considered a buttonquail (Turnicidae) but DNA studies reveal it to be the sole surviving member of an ancient lineage that diverged before the radiation of modern shorebirds. It exhibits reversed sexual dimorphism and a polyandrous breeding system.

children.name: Attagis
children.description: The larger of the two seedsnipe genera, with stout bodies, short legs, and strong bills adapted for a herbivorous diet. These are plump, grouse-like birds of the high Andes and southern Patagonia that feed almost entirely on plant material. Their cryptic plumage blends perfectly with the rocks and scree of their alpine habitat.

children.name: Thinocorus
children.description: Smaller and more delicate than Attagis, with relatively longer legs and a more terrestrial, quail-like posture. These seedsnipes are among the few birds that can subsist entirely on a vegetable diet in the harsh conditions of the high Andes and Patagonian steppe.

children.name: Thinocorus rumicivorus
children.description: The least seedsnipe (Thinocorus rumicivorus) is a xerophilic species of bird in the Thinocoridae family.

children.name: Dromas
children.description: A monotypic genus of striking black-and-white shorebird with an unusually thick, dagger-like bill adapted for crushing crabs. The Crab-plover is the only shorebird that nests in burrows dug into sandy banks, and the only member of its family. It is a colonial breeder found along the coasts of the Indian Ocean.
